newsitem.title: UK: UK Labour heads for clash with rank and file.
newsitem.headline: UK Labour heads for clash with rank and file.

text.p: Labour, swept to power just two months ago and facing a debilitated Conservative opposition, is heading for its first clash with rank and file party members.

A list of resolutions submitted by local constituency associations for the Labour party conference later this year shows an overwhelming number are opposed to plans designed to increase the leadership's control over policy-making.
Prime Minister Tony Blair shook up the party, ditching old socialist dogma and moving it to the centre in the run-up to the landslide Labour victory in the May 1 election.
But new proposals, contained in a document entitled "Labour into Power", take these reforms further.

The proposals would shift responsibility for policy-making from the annual conference to a high-level committee headed by Blair and including senior ministers who would draw on ideas developed by local policy forums at grass-roots level.

The aim is to slash the power of activists who, taking advantage of their understanding of arcane party rules forced the party sharply to the left in the 1980s and avoid clashes between the annual conference and the government over policy.
Other plans designed to reduce left-wing influence include curbs on the rights of unions at the party conference and central control over the choice of parliamentary candidates.
A list of the motions submitted to Labour's five-day conference, which starts on Monday, September 29, show 89 against the proposals and just nine broadly in favour.
Not all of the resolutions will be debated, but they show the level of disquiet felt by constituencies.
Most say that because of the election there has been insufficient time to debate the proposals and a decision should be put off for a year. But there is also outright opposition.
Stockton North constituency said in its resolution: "This conference is concerned that rank and file members are now simply being used to rubber stamp Labour Party policy.
"Policies are drafted without debate for rank and file members to accept or reject on a yes or no' basis."
But Labour leadership sources say they remain determined to push ahead with the reforms, which they say are essential if the party is to start preparing early for the necxt election.
